Key Characteristics & Etiology: Transmural myocardial ischemia/necrosis caused by complete, acute thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery following vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque rupture.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Plaque rupture exposes subendothelial collagen, causing platelet activation, aggregation, and fibrin clot formation, completely occluding coronary blood flow and producing ischemic cell death.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe, crushing retrosternal chest pain radiating to left arm/jaw, diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, anxiety, S4 gallop, hypotension/shock in massive MI.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: ST-segment elevation >= 1 mm in >= 2 contiguous leads (or new LBBB); elevated high-sensitivity Cardiac Troponin I/T; emergency Primary PCI (< 90 mins) or Thrombolysis (< 12 hrs if PCI unavailable); MONAC (Morphine, Oxygen, Nitrates, Aspirin 300mg, Clopidogrel/Ticagrelor).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Subendocardial myocardial necrosis resulting from subtotal or transient coronary arterial occlusion without persistent ST-segment elevation.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Partial thrombotic occlusion or severe demand supply mismatch leads to ischemia confined to the subendocardium, causing cellular death and cardiac biomarker release.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Anginal chest pain at rest or minimal exertion, radiating to jaw/arm, diaphoresis, shortness of breath, autonomic symptoms.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Elevated Troponin I/T (serial testing at 0 and 1-3 hrs); ECG shows ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, or normal ECG; dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor), LMWH/Fondaparinux, early invasive risk-stratified coronary angiography.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Myocardial ischemia at rest or with minimal exertion without detectable myocardial necrosis or enzyme release.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Transient coronary arterial plaque instability or vasospasm causing temporary ischemia without permanent cardiomyocyte death.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: New-onset severe angina, crescendo angina (increasing frequency/intensity), or angina at rest lasting > 20 mins; relieved poorly by rest/nitrates.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Normal cardiac Troponin levels (distinguishes UA from NSTEMI); transient ST depression or T wave inversion on ECG; Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, LMWH, beta-blockers, anti-ischemic therapy, risk stratification.

Entity / Condition: Acute Heart Failure & Acute Pulmonary Edema
Key Characteristics & Etiology: Rapid onset or worsening of heart failure symptoms requiring urgent medical evaluation and resuscitation; high acute mortality.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Sudden elevation in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) causes acute back-pressure into pulmonary capillaries, driving fluid transudation into alveoli and severely impairing gas exchange.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe acute dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), pink frothy sputum, diaphoresis, bilateral pulmonary crackles/rales, S3 gallop, elevated JVP.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Elevated BNP / NT-proBNP; CXR showing cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, Kerley B lines, bat-wing shadowing; LMNOP protocol: Loop diuretics (IV Furosemide), Morphine (for anxiety/preload reduction), Nitrates (IV/SL if SBP >= 100 mmHg), Oxygen/NIV, Position upright.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Complex clinical syndrome characterized by structural/functional cardiac impairment resulting in inadequate cardiac output or elevated intracardiac pressures.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: HFrEF (LVEF <= 40%): impaired myocardial contractility (post-MI, dilated cardiomyopathy). HFpEF (LVEF >= 50%): impaired diastolic relaxation and compliance (hypertension, LVH). Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, SNS) drives adverse ventricular remodeling.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Exertional dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, PND, peripheral edema, elevated JVP, displaced apex beat, S3 (HFrEF) or S4 (HFpEF) gallop, hepatomegaly.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Echocardiogram (LVEF measurement); elevated BNP/NT-proBNP; NYHA functional class I-IV grading; HFrEF disease-modifying therapy: ACEi/ARNI, Beta-blockers (Bisoprolol/Carvedilol), MRA (Spironolactone/Eplerenone), SGLT2 inhibitors.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Systemic immune-mediated inflammatory sequela occurring 2-4 weeks following Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis; predominantly affects children/young adults in developing regions.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M-protein and human cardiac tissue epitopes leads to cross-reactive antibody and T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium (pancarditis).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Major Jones Criteria: Carditis, Polyarthritis (migratory), Sydenham Chorea, Erythema Marginatum, Subcutaneous Nodules. Chronic RHD leads to progressive valve deformity (Mitral Stenosis > Mitral Regurgitation > Aortic valve disease).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Revised Jones Criteria (2 Major OR 1 Major + 2 Minor plus evidence of preceding GABHS infection: elevated ASO titer or positive throat swab/culture); anti-inflammatory therapy (Aspirin/corticosteroids); long-term secondary penicillin prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G every 3-4 weeks).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Narrowing of the mitral valve orifice, almost exclusively secondary to chronic Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Restricted mitral leaflet mobility and fusion of commissures obstruct left atrial emptying into LV, leading to elevated LA pressure, LA enlargement (atrial fibrillation, thrombus formation), and secondary pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, hemoptysis (bronchial vein rupture), malar flush (pink-purple patches on cheeks), systemic embolic events (stroke), signs of RV failure in late stages.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Auscultation: Loud S1, opening snap (OS) following S2, low-pitched mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at apex heard best in left lateral decubitus position; Echocardiogram (planimetry, pressure half-time, Wilkins score); Percutaneous Mitral Balloon Commissurotomy (PMBC) or valve replacement.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, most commonly affecting native or prosthetic heart valves; Staphylococcus aureus (acute/IVDU) and Streptococcus viridans (subacute/dental procedures).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Bacteremia leads to bacterial adherence on pre-existing sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations or damaged valvular endothelium, causing progressive valve destruction, regurgitation, abscess formation, and septic embolization.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Fever, night sweats, weight loss, new or changing heart murmur, peripheral vascular/immunologic stigmata: Janeway lesions (painless erythematous macules on palms/soles), Osler nodes (painful subcutaneous nodules on digits), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages), splinter hemorrhages.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Modified Duke Criteria (Major: >=2 positive blood cultures for typical organisms, Echocardiogram showing vegetation/abscess/dehiscence; Minor: predisposing heart condition/IVDU, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena); prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics (4-6 weeks); surgical intervention if severe valve failure or persistent bacteremia.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Severe acute elevation of blood pressure (typically SBP > 180 mmHg or DBP > 120 mmHg). Differentiated strictly by the presence of acute target organ damage.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Failure of vascular autoregulation under severe pressure load causes endothelial injury, fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, intravascular coagulation, and acute target organ ischemia.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Hypertensive Urgency: severe headache, epistaxis, anxiety, but NO acute organ damage. Hypertensive Emergency: BP > 180/120 with acute encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute coronary syndrome, acute pulmonary edema, eclampsia, or AKI.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Fundoscopy (papilledema, flame hemorrhages, soft exudates); serum creatinine, urinalysis, CT head, ECG, CXR. Urgency: oral antihypertensives (Labetalol, Captopril) over 24-48 hrs. Emergency: ICU admission, IV labetalol/nicardipine/sodium nitroprusside (reduce MAP by <= 25% in 1st hour).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Sustained elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure (SBP >= 140 mmHg or DBP >= 90 mmHg) without an identifiable secondary cause; accounts for 90-95% of adult hypertension cases.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Multifactorial interplay of genetic susceptibility, excessive sodium intake, sympathetic nervous system overactivity, RAAS dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and decreased endothelial nitric oxide availability.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Usually asymptomatic ('silent killer'); long-term unmanaged HTN leads to target organ damage: LV hypertrophy, coronary artery disease, stroke, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, retinopathy.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Repeated BP measurements or 24-hr Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM average >= 130/80 mmHg); screening for target organ damage (ECG for LVH, urinalysis for microalbuminuria, U&Es); 1st line pharmacological management: ACEi/ARB, Calcium Channel Blockers (Amlodipine), Thiazide-like diuretics (Indapamide).
